stem.text: Cyanoethanoic acid, CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH, is a weak organic acid.
At room temperature, CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH undergoes an acid–base reaction with NaOH(aq).
Define weak acid.

points.text: (proton donor that) partially dissociates (in aqueous solution)

explanation.text: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) donor. A weak acid is one whose molecules only partially dissociate in water, so most of it stays as undissociated HA molecules in equilibrium with a small amount of H<sup>+</sup> and A<sup>–</sup>. It is the acid molecules that dissociate to release H<sup>+</sup>; 'dissociate' is not the same as 'dissolve'.

reasoningChain: State what an acid does: donates protons.
State what makes it weak: only partially dissociates in aqueous solution.

inferredMistakes.text: Using 'dissolves' or 'partially soluble' in place of 'partially dissociates'.
Saying the H<sup>+</sup> ions partially dissociate, instead of the acid molecules.

stem.text: Sketch the pH titration curve on Figure 4.1 for the reaction of:

items: 25.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.10 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH(aq) and
0.10 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> NaOH(aq), added to excess.

stem.caption: Figure 4.1
stem.alt: Blank axes for a titration curve: pH from 0 to 14 (vertical) against volume of NaOH / cm³ from 0 to 45 (horizontal).

points.text: M1 weak acid curve starts pH 1.7 (calculation not necessary)
M3 strong alkali curve ends at pH 13

explanation.text: Equal concentrations and a 1 : 1 reaction mean the equivalence point is at 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of NaOH. Before that the curve starts at a low pH (about 1.7; cyanoethanoic acid is a fairly strong weak acid because the electron-withdrawing CN group stabilises the anion) and rises gently through the buffer region. At 25 cm<sup>3</sup> there is a sharp, near-vertical rise. After the equivalence point excess 0.10 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> NaOH controls the pH, so the curve levels off towards pH 13 and never goes above it.

reasoningChain: Find the equivalence volume: 0.10 × 25.00 = 0.10 × V, so V = 25 cm<sup>3</sup>.
Start the curve at a low pH (about 1.7) for the weak acid.
Draw the steep vertical section at 25 cm<sup>3</sup>.
Level off at pH 13 (0.10 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> OH<sup>–</sup>) by 45 cm<sup>3</sup>.

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing the steep section at the wrong volume, or with a gradual slope rather than a near-vertical rise.
Letting the curve keep rising to pH 14 or above, instead of levelling off at pH 13.
Starting the curve at pH 1, as for a 0.10 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> strong acid.

stem.text: Write the overall ionic equation for the neutralisation of CH2(CN)COOH(aq) by NaOH(aq) in 4(a)(ii).
Include state symbols.

explanation.text: Every neutralisation of an acid by an alkali comes down to H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + OH<sup>–</sup>(aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O(l); Na<sup>+</sup> and the cyanoethanoate ion are spectator ions. The ER reports that an equation written from the undissociated acid, CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH(aq) + OH<sup>–</sup>(aq) → CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COO<sup>–</sup>(aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O(l), was also credited.

reasoningChain: Remove the spectator ions from the full equation.
Write H<sup>+</sup>(aq) + OH<sup>–</sup>(aq) → H<sub>2</sub>O(l) with state symbols.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing the full molecular equation with NaOH and the sodium salt, which is not an ionic equation.
Leaving out the state symbols the question asks for.

stem.text: Suggest the formula of the organic product when CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH(aq) is heated under reflux with NaOH(aq).

explanation.text: Heating under reflux with NaOH(aq) does two things. The COOH group is neutralised to COO<sup>–</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>, and the nitrile group is hydrolysed: –CN + OH<sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O → –COO<sup>–</sup> + NH<sub>3</sub>. The alkaline solution keeps both groups as carboxylate salts, so the product is disodium propanedioate, CH<sub>2</sub>(COONa)<sub>2</sub>. No acidification is mentioned, so the free acid is not formed.

reasoningChain: Reflux with alkali hydrolyses the CN group to a carboxylate.
The COOH group is neutralised by NaOH.
Both groups end up as COONa: CH<sub>2</sub>(COONa)<sub>2</sub>.

inferredMistakes.text: Converting only the COOH group to COONa and leaving CN unchanged, giving CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COONa.
Giving the free acid CH<sub>2</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub>, which would need a later acidification step.

stem.text: CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH is very soluble in water because it can form hydrogen bonds with water.
Complete Figure 4.2 to show one hydrogen bond between a molecule of CH2(CN)COOH and a molecule of H2O.
Label the hydrogen bond clearly, and show any relevant partial charges and lone pairs of electrons.

stem.caption: Figure 4.2
stem.alt: Displayed formula of cyanoethanoic acid: N≡C–CH2–C(=O)–O–H, with the two H atoms on the central carbon drawn above and below it.

points.text: M2 from lone pair on any oxygen to H atom attached to O
M3 with three correct successive partial charges across two molecules

explanation.text: A hydrogen bond forms between an H atom bonded to a very electronegative atom (here O) and a lone pair on an O (or N) atom in another molecule. Two arrangements work: the O–H hydrogen of the acid bonding to a lone pair on the water O, or a water O–H hydrogen bonding to a lone pair on the C=O or O–H oxygen of the acid. The H atoms on the CH<sub>2</sub> carbon cannot take part, because C–H is not polar enough.

Partial charges: show three in a row across the two molecules, for example O<sup>δ–</sup>–H<sup>δ+</sup> ⋯ :O<sup>δ–</sup>. Draw the hydrogen bond as a dashed line, clearly different from the covalent bonds, labelled 'hydrogen bond', and drawn from the lone pair to the H.

reasoningChain: Pick an O–H hydrogen (acid or water) and an O lone pair on the other molecule.
Draw the lone pair on that O.
Draw a dashed line from the lone pair to the H and label it hydrogen bond.
Mark δ– on the first O, δ+ on the H and δ– on the lone-pair O.

inferredMistakes.text: Forming the hydrogen bond to one of the CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens.
Leaving out the lone pair on the electronegative atom.
Showing fewer than three partial charges, or drawing the hydrogen bond like a covalent bond.

stem.text: Figure 4.3 shows a synthesis of CH<sub>2</sub>(CN)COOH.

stem.caption: Figure 4.3
stem.alt: Reaction scheme: chloroethanoic acid (Cl–CH2–COOH, skeletal formula) reacts with KCN dissolved in ethanol (arrow) to give cyanoethanoic acid (NC–CH2–COOH). Below the reactant is the cyanide ion drawn as C≡N with a negative charge on C; below the product is Cl⁻.

stem.text: The reaction mechanism of the synthesis in Figure 4.3 has a single step.
Complete Figure 4.3 to show this mechanism. Include lone pairs, charges, dipoles and curly arrows as appropriate.

points.text: M1 curly arrow from lone pair on C of CN– to (δ+)C of C—Cl
M2 correct dipole of δ+C—Clδ– AND curly arrow from bond to Cl

explanation.text: A single step means SN2. The C–Cl bond is polar (Cδ+–Clδ–) because Cl is more electronegative. The cyanide ion attacks with the lone pair on its carbon atom (which carries the negative charge): one curly arrow goes from that lone pair to the δ+ carbon. At the same time the C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically: a second curly arrow goes from the middle of the C–Cl bond to Cl, which leaves as Cl–. The new bond is C–C, which is why the arrow must start on carbon, not nitrogen.

reasoningChain: Mark the dipole δ+ on C and δ– on Cl.
Draw a lone pair and negative charge on the C of CN<sup>–</sup>.
Curly arrow 1: from the C lone pair to the δ+ carbon.
Curly arrow 2: from the C–Cl bond to Cl.

inferredMistakes.text: Starting the curly arrow from the N of the cyanide ion instead of the lone pair on C.
Leaving out the δ+/δ– dipole on the C–Cl bond.
Ending the arrows somewhere that does not show clearly which atom the electrons move to.

stem.text: Identify the nucleophile in Figure 4.3.

explanation.text: A nucleophile is a species that donates a lone pair to an electron-deficient (δ+) atom. Here it is the cyanide ion, CN<sup>–</sup>, from KCN. 'Nitrile' is the name of the –C≡N functional group in an organic molecule, not of the attacking ion.

reasoningChain: Find the species that brings a lone pair to the δ+ carbon: CN<sup>–</sup>.
Name it as the cyanide ion.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'nitrile' or 'nitrile group' instead of the cyanide ion.
Giving KCN, which includes the spectator K<sup>+</sup>.

stem.text: Identify the mechanism of the reaction in Figure 4.3.

explanation.text: The cyanide nucleophile replaces Cl on the carbon of the halogenoalkane-type C–Cl group, so the mechanism is nucleophilic substitution. Because it happens in a single step (from (c)(i)), it is the SN2 type. The carbon attacked is primary, which also favours SN2.

reasoningChain: The attacking species is a nucleophile.
Cl is replaced: substitution.
Answer: nucleophilic substitution (S<sub>N</sub>2).

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'free-radical substitution' or 'electrophilic substitution', so the type of substitution is wrong.

stem.text: Figure 4.4 describes a sequence of reactions, starting with CH2(CN)COOH, to form E.

stem.caption: Figure 4.4
stem.alt: Reaction sequence: NC–CH2–COOH reacts with C2H5OH and H⁺ (step 1) to give NC–CH2–COOC2H5; this reacts with HCHO (step 2) to give E, CH2=C(CN)–COOC2H5 (ethyl 2-cyanopropenoate), drawn as a skeletal formula.

stem.text: Identify the type of reaction that occurs in step 1.

explanation.text: In step 1 the carboxylic acid reacts with ethanol, with H<sup>+</sup> as catalyst, to form an ester and water. Two molecules join and a small molecule (H<sub>2</sub>O) is lost, so it is a condensation reaction (also called esterification).

reasoningChain: Acid + alcohol → ester + water.
Two molecules joining with loss of water is condensation.

inferredMistakes.text: Answering 'addition' or 'substitution', missing that water is eliminated.

stem.text: Name HCHO, the reactant used in step 2.

explanation.text: HCHO is the simplest aldehyde: one carbon atom with a C=O group and two H atoms. The systematic name uses the stem meth- (one carbon) and the aldehyde suffix -al: methanal. ('Formaldehyde' is the non-systematic name.)

reasoningChain: Recognise HCHO as an aldehyde with one carbon.
Name it: meth- + -al = methanal.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing 'methanol', which is the alcohol CH<sub>3</sub>OH.

stem.text: Deduce the molecular formula of E.

explanation.text: E is CH2=C(CN)COOC2H5. Count each atom: C: 1 (CH2) + 1 (C=) + 1 (CN) + 1 (C=O) + 2 (C2H5) = 6; H: 2 + 5 = 7; N: 1; O: 2. A molecular formula is only the atom counts, C6H7NO2, not a structural formula.

reasoningChain: Write E out in full from the skeletal formula, including the hidden H atoms.
Count C, H, N and O.
Write the counts in the order C, H, then the other elements alphabetically.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing a structural formula such as CH<sub>2</sub>C(CN)COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> instead of the molecular formula.
Missing the hydrogen atoms on the =CH<sub>2</sub> end, which are not drawn in the skeletal formula.

stem.text: E can be polymerised to form F.
Draw the structure of one repeat unit of polymer F.

points.text: repeat unit: two carbons in the chain (one with two H atoms, one with COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> and CN), with extended (dashed) bonds at each end

markScheme.note: The MS answer is a drawn displayed repeat unit; shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Repeat unit of polymer F: two chain carbons joined by a single bond with dashed bonds at both ends; the left carbon has two H atoms, the right carbon has COOC2H5 above and CN below.

explanation.text: E is an alkene, so it forms an addition polymer. The C=C opens to a single C–C bond, and each carbon makes a new bond to the next repeat unit. Only the two carbons that were in the C=C go into the chain; the CN and COOC2H5 groups stay as side groups on the same carbon. The bonds at each end are drawn extended (or through brackets) to show the unit continues.

reasoningChain: Find the C=C in E: CH<sub>2</sub>=C(CN)COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>.
Change it to a single bond and add an open bond at each end.
Keep H, H on one carbon and CN, COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> on the other.

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing the end bonds the same as the other bonds, so it is not clear the structure continues.
Putting the ester or nitrile carbon into the main chain, or joining a side group to the wrong carbon.
Keeping the C=C double bond in the repeat unit.

Main absorptions: a medium double peak near 3000 cm⁻¹, a sharp narrow peak near 2250 cm⁻¹, a very strong peak near 1750 cm⁻¹, a strong peak near 1550 cm⁻¹, and several strong peaks between about 1450 and 1000 cm⁻¹.

stem.text: Using the information given in Table 4.1, identify with a cross (×) on Figure 4.5 an absorption that can be used to monitor the progress of the polymerisation of E to form F.
Explain your answer with reference to the relevant bond.

markScheme.note: The MS prints three bullets for 2 marks.

explanation.text: Addition polymerisation uses up the C=C bond of E, while the C≡N, C=O and C–O bonds are still there in F. So the absorption to watch is the C=C stretch (Table 4.1: 1500–1680 cm–1), the strong peak at about 1550 cm–1 just to the right of the very strong C=O peak (about 1750 cm–1). It gets smaller and disappears as the polymer forms. Choosing the C=O or C≡N peak would not work, because those bonds are in both monomer and polymer.

reasoningChain: Decide which bond is lost in addition polymerisation: C=C.
Find the C=C range in Table 4.1 (1500–1680 cm<sup>–1</sup>) and put the cross on the peak in that range.
Explain that this peak disappears as E is converted into F.

inferredMistakes.text: Choosing the very strong C=O peak near 1740 cm<sup>–1</sup>, which is still present in the polymer.
Identifying the C=C peak but not saying that it disappears as the monomer becomes polymer.
